results.title: The Compute Price Reset: Priced Like Credit - DalalBytes
results.author: Prakash Damodaran
highlights:
For two years, the price of rented AI compute did one thing. It fell. H100 rates that spiked above $8 per GPU-hour in the 2023 shortage slid through 2024 as supply caught up, and in June 2025 AWS cut on-demand pricing for its H100 P5 instances by 44%, with comparable reductions following at Google Cloud and Azure. Budgeting for 2026 on the assumption that the slide would continue was the consensus move. It was also wrong.

results.title: AWS vs Azure vs GCP Cloud GPU Pricing [2026]
results.author: Sana Rahman
highlights:
AWS maps its Nvidia GPU families onto a small set of EC2 instance types. According to AWS’s own documentation, the ml.p5.48xlarge family is built around H100 GPUs, while ml.p5e.48xlarge and ml.p5en.48xlarge carry H200 GPUs. The newer P6-B200 family moves to Blackwell-generation B200 GPUs, AWS also lists P6-B300 instances built around B300 GPUs as a newer, higher-tier option, and a P6e-GB200 UltraServer tier built around Nvidia’s GB200 NVL72 rack-scale system for the largest training clusters. Each of these families is purchasable On-Demand, through Spot Instances, or through Savings Plans, and all of them are also eligible for Capacity Block reservations.

...

What AWS has not done, at least not in any officially confirmed source available as of October 23, 2026, is publish a flat on-demand hourly price for P5, P5e, P5en or P6-B200. Capacity Block pricing is explicitly dynamic, and AWS’s public materials direct buyers to request a quote or check the Capacity Blocks console rather than read a rate card.

...

| GPU | AWS (published rate) |

...

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100, single GPU | No flat rate published; Capacity Blocks price dynamically | $6.98/hour, NC40ads H100 v5, East US, captured Oct. 19, 2026 | Not published |
| H100, 8-GPU node | No flat rate published | $98.32/hour ($12.29/GPU-hour), ND96isr H100 v5, East US, captured Oct. 19, 2026 | Not published |
| H200, 8-GPU node | No flat rate published | No flat on-demand VM rate confirmed in official sources | Not published |
| B200, per GPU-hour (Capacity Block) | $14.208/hour, effective Oct. 7, 2026, up from $12.355/hour (about a 15% increase) | Not offered / not confirmed | Not published; A4 uses Flex-start scheduling instead of a flat rate |

Independent GPU-rental trackers fill in some of the gaps, but their numbers are estimates rather than official list prices and should be read that way. GPU-pricing trackers reportedly placed AWS P5 H100 Capacity Block pricing around $5.97 per GPU-hour, effective October 7, 2026, and P5e/P5en H200 pricing between $6.87 and $7.895 per GPU-hour, effective October 7, 2026, though AWS itself does not publish those as fixed rates. Axis Intelligence’s October 22, 2026 comparison floated per-hour figures for Google Cloud H200 (A3 Ultra) and B200 (A4), but the same tracker found no confirmed on-demand price for those configurations, since they were marked as not available for direct purchase, so no official Google Cloud rate exists for either one. Treat any number below these published figures as directional until a provider confirms it on an official pricing page.

...

## The October 7 AWS B200 Price Hike, Explained

The single clearest pricing move any of the three providers made in the last three months was AWS’s. Effective October 7, 2026, AWS raised its P6-B200 Capacity Block price from $12.355 to $14.208 per accelerator-hour, an increase of approximately 15%, according to GPU-pricing trackers Axis Intelligence and Dev.to’s FastGPU column, which independently captured the same before-and-after figures. For an eight-GPU P6-B200 node, the current instance-hour rate is about $113.666, a noticeable jump in monthly spend for teams running sustained training jobs.

AWS frames Capacity Block pricing as dynamic by design, moving with supply and demand rather than sitting on a fixed card, so a mid-quarter increase is consistent with how the product is supposed to work. It is also a useful data point for the “which cloud is cheapest” question: it shows that even the provider with the most reservation flexibility, AWS, is not necessarily the cheapest or the most stable option for Blackwell-class capacity right now. Teams planning a long B200 training run in Q4 2026 should budget for the possibility of another adjustment before their reservation window closes, since trackers reported this was not the first GPU list-price increase AWS made in recent months.

A price-list change (Glue 6.0, S3 Vectors, the GPU management fees, Network Firewall, a Bedrock model price) keeps the usage types and lowers the rate. The check is therefore the rate per usage type on either side of the effective date: `line_item_unblended_rate` grouped by `line_item_usage_type` in CUR 2.0, `ListUnitPrice` and `ContractedUnitPrice` in the FOCUS export. A reduction that starts mid-month shows as two rates for one usage type in one month. Nothing has to be done, unless the reduction applies only to a new version, as with Glue 6.0: then the job has to move first, and it pays the old rate until it does. A promotional price with an end date, as for GPT-5.6 Sol, returns to the list price after that day unless AWS extends it. Where the columns sit is in the AWS Cost and Usage Report and FOCUS columns.

results.title: AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks price increase 2026: p5.48xlarge goes from $31.464 to $47.757 an hour
results.author: Fieldnote Labs
highlights:
AWS raised the price of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML four times in 2026. In US East (Ohio), p5.48xlarge went from $31.464 to $47.757 an hour per instance. p6-b200.48xlarge went from $74.88 to $113.666. p4d.24xlarge went from $11.8 to $13.57 in October. trn1.32xlarge stayed at $9.532. We do not track AWS on SaaS Price Watch yet. These rates come from the AWS pricing page and archived copies of it. See the AWS public IPv4 price change.

## Old and new prices

Hourly rate per instance in US East (Ohio), in US dollars, as AWS lists them on each date.

| Instance | December 24, 2025 | January 3, 2026 | April 15, 2026 | August 25, 2026 | October 10, 2026 and now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| p5.48xlarge (8 x H100) | $31.464 | $31.464 | $34.608 | $41.528 | $47.757 |
| p5e.48xlarge (8 x H200) | $34.608 | $39.799 | $39.799 | $47.76 | $54.924 |
| p5en.48xlarge (8 x H200) | $36.184 | $41.612 | $45.768 | $54.920 | $63.158 |
| p6-b200.48xlarge (8 x B200) | $74.88 | $74.88 | $82.368 | $98.84 | $113.666 |
| p4d.24xlarge (8 x A100) | $11.8 | $11.8 | $11.8 | $11.8 | $13.57 |
| trn1.32xlarge (16 x Trainium) | $9.532 | $9.532 | $9.532 | $9.532 | $9.532 |

Per accelerator, the page now lists p5.48xlarge at $5.970 an hour, up from $3.933 on December 24, 2025. p6-b200.48xlarge is at $14.208, up from $9.36.

Our math: from December 24, 2025 to now, p5.48xlarge is up $16.293 an hour (52%), p5e.48xlarge $20.316 (59%), p5en.48xlarge $26.974 (75%), and p6-b200.48xlarge $38.786 (52%). p4d.24xlarge is up $1.77 (15%). Each step was 10%, 15%, or 20% on the instances that changed. A 24 hour block of one p5.48xlarge now costs $1,146.17, up from $755.14. A one week block of 168 hours costs $8,023.18, up from $5,285.95.

...

## What AWS said

The pricing page says "Reservation prices are updated regularly based on trends in supply and demand for EC2 Capacity Blocks." It now says "The current prices are scheduled to be updated next in January, 2027." The page says "The reservation fee is charged up front at the time you schedule the reservation." It adds "Your Capacity Block is charged at the prevailing rate at the time of purchase, even if the Capacity Block is scheduled to start after the price is updated."

## Who it hits and when

Anyone who books a new Capacity Block pays the rate on the page at purchase. A block bought before an update keeps the rate it was bought at, by the AWS wording above. By the archived copies, the updates landed between December 24, 2025 and January 3, 2026, between March 31 and April 15, 2026, between July 4 and August 25, 2026, and between October 1 and October 10, 2026. The next scheduled update is in January, 2027.

results.title: AWS is raising GPU instance prices by ~20% on July 1 — and quietly keeping its own Trainium chips at
results.author: Paul Nugent
highlights:
AWS is raising GPU instance prices by ~20% on July 1 — and quietly keeping its own Trainium chips at the same price.

This is the most important AI infrastructure pricing story of the year, and the signal is unmistakable.

The move: ~20% price increase on EC2 Capacity Block reservations for Nvidia GPU instances, effective July 1. AWS cited "supply and demand dynamics" — meaning the global compute crunch has gotten severe enough that AWS believes customers will pay more without leaving.

The critical detail: Trainium pricing is unchanged.

AWS now operates two parallel compute economics tracks:

🔹 NVIDIA TRACK: +20% — you absorb Nvidia's pricing power, supply constraints, AND AWS's margin protection layered on top.

🔹 TRAINIUM TRACK: flat — Amazon subsidizes the economics because every workload that migrates to Trainium deepens lock-in to the AWS ecosystem.
